prompt: Why does a postmortem that looks for blame learn nothing else, by the lesson?
hint: What do people do when they expect punishment?

choices.text: Because blame is illegal under labour law
choices.why: Not a legal argument.

choices.text: Because the person blamed always leaves the company soon after
choices.why: Not the argument made.

choices.text: Everybody else stops telling the truth
choices.why: Right: accounts become self-protective, and the detail is lost.

choices.text: Because blame takes too long to assign
choices.why: Time is not the issue.

prompt: What did the blameless reading of 6 March find about Paulo's decision?

choices.text: It made sense by everything he could see
choices.why: Right: the runbook said to run it when zones changed, and said nothing about peak.

choices.text: He should have checked the dashboard first
choices.why: Nothing told him to, and the dashboard did not show connections.

choices.text: He was not authorised to run the backfill
choices.why: He was; it was in the runbook.

choices.text: He ignored a rule against running jobs at peak
choices.why: There was no such rule; that was the hole.

prompt: What does "blameless" not mean, by the lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: That nobody is accountable
choices.why: Right: accountability moves to who will change what.

choices.text: That names are never written in the timeline
choices.why: Right: the timeline says Paulo started the job.

choices.text: That deliberate sabotage is a systems problem
choices.why: Right: that is conduct, handled outside.

choices.text: That the review asks why an action made sense
choices.why: That is exactly what blameless means.

prompt: Sidney Dekker's principle that people's actions make sense from where they stood is called local ___.
What makes a postmortem timeline more than a log?

choices.text: Screenshots of every dashboard involved
choices.why: Evidence, not the decisions.

choices.text: Timestamps to the second
choices.why: Precision helps; it does not explain decisions.

choices.text: What people could see, and decided
choices.why: Right: the decisions and what they rested on.

choices.text: A section naming who made each mistake
choices.why: That is blame, not learning.

prompt: From 19:09 to the alert at 19:16, for how many minutes did nothing measure the cause?
What question should every timeline be read once with, by the lesson?

choices.text: "Who should have caught this?"
choices.why: That looks for blame.

choices.text: "Not knowing the end, would I have known better?"
choices.why: Right: where the honest answer is no, the lesson is about the system.

choices.text: "How much did it cost the company?"
choices.why: Useful elsewhere; not the hindsight check.

choices.text: "What would an expert have done instead, with the same information?"
choices.why: An expert with hindsight is the problem.

prompt: Which timeline line follows the lesson's advice?

choices.text: "Paulo ran the job during peak"
choices.why: The judgement hides in "during peak".

choices.text: "Paulo carelessly started the job without checking the time of day"
choices.why: An evaluation, and blame.

choices.text: "Paulo starts the backfill; the runbook does not mention peak"
choices.why: Right: both facts, and the reader sees where the problem is.

choices.text: "Someone started a job"
choices.why: Hiding a name the timeline needs is not blamelessness either.

prompt: How many holes lined up on 6 March, by the lesson's list?
What weakness of the five whys does the lesson name?

choices.text: It follows one single chain, and whoever is asking picks which one
choices.why: Right: which is how the chain in the lesson ended at Paulo.

choices.text: Five is too few to reach the real cause
choices.why: The number is not the problem.

choices.text: It takes too long in a review meeting with many people present
choices.why: Time is not the weakness named.

choices.text: It was designed for factories and does not apply to software
choices.why: It applies; its shape is the issue.

prompt: Which is a finding written as a property of the system?

choices.text: "Human error"
choices.why: Ends the inquiry where it should start.

choices.text: "Logistics was careless with the database on a busy Friday evening"
choices.why: Blame by team.

choices.text: "Nobody set a connection limit for any of the services"
choices.why: Invites "who should have?"

choices.text: "The database has no per-service connection limit"
choices.why: Right: it invites a fix.

prompt: Which single change would, on its own, have kept checkout up on 6 March? Choose all that apply.
hint: Close any one hole on the path.

choices.text: A per-service connection limit on the database
choices.why: Yes: the backfill would be slow and checkout fine.

choices.text: A runbook line against running it at peak
choices.why: Yes: it would have run at 23:00.

choices.text: A cap on how many connections the job opens
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: A faster checkout deploy pipeline
choices.why: There was no deploy involved.

prompt: Match each action from 6 March to its kind.
Why is "be more careful" not an action?

choices.text: It is too harsh on the people involved
choices.why: Tone is not the problem.

choices.text: It belongs in the timeline instead
choices.why: It belongs nowhere.

choices.text: Careful people still make mistakes, so it is false
choices.why: True, and not why it fails as an action.

choices.text: It names no change, owner, date or ticket
choices.why: Right: it cannot be done or checked.

prompt: Before the 6 March review, what percentage of postmortem actions were done by their due date?
Why does the lesson treat Paulo owning the fix to the job as a good sign?

choices.text: Nobody else was available that month
choices.why: Not the reason.

choices.text: It is his punishment for starting the job
choices.why: The lesson says trust rather than penance.

choices.text: He is closest to the system around it
choices.why: Right: asking him is a sign of trust.

choices.text: The rules say whoever triggers an incident fixes it
choices.why: No such rule.

prompt: Match each culture to how it treats messengers.
What question does the lesson suggest asking the newest engineer to read a team's culture?

choices.text: "Do you like working here?"
choices.why: Too general to reveal how failure is treated.

choices.text: "Have you read our postmortems, and do you think they are useful?"
choices.why: Reading them says little about what reporting costs.

choices.text: "If you broke production tomorrow, what would happen to you?"
choices.why: Right: the answer is the culture.

choices.text: "How many incidents did we have last quarter, and how bad were they?"
choices.why: A number, not the culture.

prompt: Why did Marola write up the April near miss?

choices.text: It showed an action working
choices.why: Right: the best argument for the next action.

choices.text: To find out who started the second backfill
choices.why: Not a blame exercise.

choices.text: To show leadership the team had been busy
choices.why: Not the purpose.

choices.text: Because the policy requires a write-up for every job run
choices.why: No such policy.

prompt: A first draft of a postmortem says: "Root cause: Diego merged without running the tests." Following this lesson, what should the review ask first?

choices.text: Whether Diego should keep merge rights
choices.why: A sanction, not a question.

choices.text: How much the incident cost, to set the severity
choices.why: Useful, and not the first question about the cause.

choices.text: Why it made sense to him, and what allowed it
choices.why: Right: local rationality, then the holes in the system.

choices.text: Who reviewed Diego's change and approved it
choices.why: Moves the blame one person along.
